references.text: The same context regarding the holy anointing oil that must not be made for personal use - a parallel command concerning holiness reserved for the Lord
Prohibition against offering foreign incense on the altar of incense - emphasizing that the incense is holy and reserved for the Lord's service
The concept of something being most holy to the Lord - the same principle of holiness that sets it apart for God
Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and died - illustrating the seriousness of misusing what is holy to the Lord
Moses burns fragrant incense on the altar as the Lord commanded - correct use of the holy incense
Incense in heaven represents the prayers of the saints - the holy function of incense continues as a symbol in the New Testament
Both verses illustrate the principle that holy gifts must be free from human additions or personal initiatives to be acceptable to God.
Both verses link the requirement for personal holiness directly to the role of carrying forward God's holy offerings.
The verse explains the theological basis for the requirement of holiness in 30:37: God's holy things require that those who serve them are dedicated to Him.
Both verses illustrate the consequence of dedicating something to the Lord: it becomes holy and can no longer be used for personal purposes.
Both verses emphasize that holy things are reserved for God's service and must not be used or owned privately.
